Stay out of Excel Hell

This week I thought we would combine the FP&A Guy's Tech Tip and stay out of Excel Hell Together. ​ A great way to improve your Excel skills is to use Generative AI. With that in mind I recently asked four different LLM's (ChatGPT, Claude AI, Gemini, CoPilot the following questions:

​

​

What are the Top 10 Most Useful Excel Functions

​

​

What I found interesting is every LLM and every different version of the same company returned a different list. ​ Below is what I learned from the experience:

​

​

➡ Every LLM will return different answers it is a good idea to use more than one LLM when researching a subject.

​

➡ Not a single LLM included a Dynamic Array formula beyond Xlookup which shows they do not always have the most recent information.

​

➡ Little things matter. Some lists included SUMIF, and others SUMIFS. The IFS formula, in general, is more powerful as it manages multiple criteria instead of just one criteria

​

➡ If we change the question to what are the TOP 10 most popular functions, we get a different answer. How you ask the question matters.

​

➡ Some of the tools provided multiple similar functions together, giving more than ten answers, while others did not.

​

➡ Only two formulas appeared in all four lists. Remember, asking multiple people a question is a way to get the best answer, same with LLMs. As Jim Cook taught me, the smartest person in the room is the room, not

any individual in the room. The same is true when it comes to LLM's.

​

​

Remember, Generative AI can help you learn Excel and keep you out of Excel Hell, but it requires asking the right questions and questioning the answers. ​ For example, if you asked me my top 10 functions to learn it would be different than any of the ones above with some overlap with all four.

Business Partner's Corner

Great Finance business partners are always learning! I have worked with some fantastic CFOs who despite their position on the organization chart are excited to learn.

​

They are open to different and potentially new ways of working.

​

Here are five ways to learn.

​

1) Find a mentor or coach. Someone you admire and want to be like. I was shy in my early days in Finance and would not ask. I have learned to get past my fears and just ask! It has been such a game changer for me.

​

2) Read! Whether it is books, articles, white papers, it is a winning skill. Warren Buffett sits in his office and reads all day. Bill Gates takes reading vacations! Oprah talks about reading being a superpower!

​

3) Listen to podcasts. There is a wealth of phenomenal free information out there. Here are three of my favourites:

​

FP&A Tomorrow – Paul Barnhurst ​

The School of Greatness - Lewis Howes. ​

​Diary of a CEO – Steven Bartlett.

​

4) Form or join a mastermind group. This is a game changing approach. Get together regularly with like minded folks who want to learn. It is a great way to share perspectives and hold each other in a supportive way.

​

​

5) Get out of your cube!  This is about learning the business from many angles. Talking to cross functional stakeholders and being curious. It could mean getting out to factories in a manufacturing environment.

​

​

Ongoing learning sets you up for success and is FUN!

Ron's Recommendations

Twelve Pillars, Jim Rohn & Chris Widener

Jim Rohn is the father of personal development! He mentored Tony Robbins before Robbins became a legend. I often listen to his melodic voice on YouTube when I need inspiration, guidance, or a kick in the behind.

​

This short book starts with the main character Michael Jones feeling like his life is “crud.” He felt like he was a failure. To add to his misery, his car broke down. He then had a chance encounter with a person who would change his life. Charlie ended up fixing his car and helping him turn around his life with several lessons over the next few weeks.

​

The book has 12 chapters/pillars, and each one is a pillar that helped Michael transform his life!

​

  1. A chance encounter.
  2. Live a life of health.
  3. The gift of relationships.
  4. Achieve your goals.
  5. The proper use of time.
  6. Surround yourself with the best people.
  7. Be a lifelong learner.
  8. All of life is Sales.
  9. Income seldom exceeds personal development.
  10. All communication brings the common ground of understanding.
  11. The world can always use one more leader.
  12. Leave a legacy.

​

Let’s go deeper into three of these pillars:

​

8) All of life is Sales (successfully influencing others).

​

How does this apply to Finance? In short, Sales is about influence and in Finance this is an important skill. So how do you learn the art and skill of influencing others?

​

They must perceive you as a person of talent and virtue with strong character. Learn the business from all angles (well beyond the numbers). Know your stuff. Become an expert in your area of the business. Talk to lots of people. Curiosity is such an important skill and as Finance professionals we are tempted to hibernate in our cubicles. Be persistent and never take ‘no’ for an answer. This is a secret to a successful sales career where rejection is often experienced more than winning the sale. Being persistent despite setbacks is a winning trait for anyone.

​

Imagine if Finance folks embraced these concepts. Our influence would skyrocket!

​

7 & 9) Be a lifelong learner. Income seldom exceeds personal development.

​

“Formal education will make you a living. Self-education will make you a fortune.”

​

Self education is a mindset of always being curious and having a huge appetite to learn. It is having a sense of curiosity and a beginner’s mindset. It is about constantly growing and improving. It is about never feeling like you know it all.

​

The book talks about the mainstays of learning:

​

Reading books or listening to podcasts (opens us up to vast worlds to explore and understand). Learn from successful people through observation. There is a common saying out there that we are the average of the five people we surround ourselves with. Constantly reflect and learn from your own experiences and learn what went right and wrong.

​

“Income seldom exceeds personal development. If you want to make a million dollars, you had better grow to the point where you are a million-dollar person.”

I first met Jack when Datarails asked me to interview him for the FP&A Today podcast since that time I have had the pleasure of chatting with him several times and have tome to realize he is a leading voice in the world of Financial Planning & Analysis (FP&A).

​

With his extensive background in corporate finance and his keen insights into market trends, Jack has consistently provided valuable, actionable guidance that helps businesses optimize their financial performance and strategic planning. His influence extends through his prolific writing, engaging talks, and active participation in industry forums, where he empowers professionals with the tools and understanding needed to navigate complex financial landscapes. Jacks's contributions have not only shaped best practices but have also set new benchmarks in the effectiveness of financial planning and analysis.

​

Jack has written several books on FP&A and I would highly recommend checking them out. His books include:

​

​

  • Financial Management: Partner in Driving Performance and Value (Wiley Finance)
  • Financial Planning & Analysis and Performance Management (Wiley Finance)
  • Performance Dashboards and Analysis for Value Creation

​

We highly recommend checking out one of Jack’s books and/or his podcast episodes on FP&A Today as he is a great person to learn from. ​ ​
